source.title: Two models of double descent for weak features
source.authors: Mikhail Belkin; Daniel J. Hsu; Ji Xu

record.tranche_reason: The study derives and evaluates risk-versus-feature-count behavior in two random-feature regression models, using an exact mathematical analysis rather than the original empirical approach.
record.gate_note: The paper's own results are the Gaussian-model risk formulas and the Fourier-model asymptotic analysis and simulation. Figure 2 compares prescient feature selection, but the figure does not provide extractable values or a clear textual account of the full curve shape. Statements about neural networks and optimal ridge regularization attributed to other works are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The paper derives exact (Gaussian) and asymptotic (Fourier) risk curves for least-norm least squares as feature count p varies. It shows the risk diverges near p = n and falls again beyond n. This bears directly on V4 for a non-deep model class, using mathematical analysis rather than the originals' empirical method.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that risk is infinite around p = n and decreases beyond it in both models. With high signal-to-noise, the minimum risk is reached at p > n. Under prescient selection, the optimum is at p ≤ n.
record.recipe_differences: The paper gives exact and asymptotic mathematical risk analyses for least-squares/least-norm predictors in Gaussian and Fourier random-feature models, rather than testing the original broad empirical set of models.
record.method_sensitivity: The results differ between random and prescient feature selection. In the Gaussian random-selection model, whether the minimum risk occurs at p = D depends on the stated signal-to-noise condition.
record.peer_reviewed: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science
record.problems: The evidence concerns two simplified linear regression feature models, not deep networks. The Fourier result is asymptotic, and its finite example uses one randomly chosen β and 10 random choices of S and T, with values reported only in a plot. The paper does not test epochs or vary sample size.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 is an illustration of the Gaussian random-selection risk already represented by the exact formulas in R4–R6; no separate numeric values are stated.

untested.parts: Sample size n is not varied as the axis of interest.
Only two linear random-feature regression models with least-norm fitting. Other model classes are not tested.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak location.
Label-noise dependence, multiple peaks and optimal regularization are not tested. The ridge result is cited from Hastie et al., not shown here.

missing.what: Condition under which the global minimum lies past the threshold: SNR ||β||²/σ² > D/(D−n−1) gives minimum risk at p = D. Under prescient selection, the optimum is at some p ≤ n. This is currently only in the notes of R6 and R9.
missing.locator: Section 2.1, text after Corollary 1; Section 1 intro

record.verdict_notes: This is not one of the original sources, though it shares authors with arXiv:1812.11118. The Fourier model is noise-free yet the risk still diverges near p = n. There, misspecification (unused features) plays the role of noise. This is relevant context for V6 but is not a test of label-noise dependence. R9 (prescient selection) is correctly cannot_determine: the text says only that the optimum is at p ≤ n, and the figure gives no values.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test deep networks.
Training epochs or training-time risk curves are not tested.
The number of training samples is not varied to test whether more data raises test error.
The study tests two specific linear regression feature models, not general model classes.
No single measure of effective complexity is tested as a predictor of peak location.
The study does not test noise-driven peaks, multiple descent, or optimally tuned regularization; the ridge-regularization point is attributed to another work.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective parameter count or test whether this changes the curve to an ordinary U shape.

tranche.reason: Exact Gaussian and asymptotic Fourier risk analyses address the double-descent question through a different method from the original empirical demonstrations.

source_check.notes: Gaussian results assume σ>0; the monotonic random-selection discussion assumes D>n+1. The Fourier theorem analyzes only ρp>ρn, and its subsets are sampled by independent Bernoulli membership.

statements.correction: Gaussian random selection: risk = +∞ for n−1 ≤ p ≤ n+1; risk decreases for p ≥ n+2 when D > n+1. Supplied header: arXiv:1903.07571v2, October 2020; SIAM publication and review status not stated.
statements.problem: The Gaussian risk claims are supported. The assertion that this supplied text has a reviewed SIAM header is unsupported: its header identifies an arXiv version.
